description: Building EarthSOC Sentinel - a SIEM-inspired planetary telemetry and anomaly detection dashboard! Instead of basic charts, we ingest real NASA Earthdata time-series metrics into SQL and Python to baseline normal environmental behavior, filter false positives, and trigger automated Critical/High/Medium severity alerts for unusual climate and thermal spikes. Open to virtual or in-person Chicago teammates!
summary:
EarthSOC Sentinel applies a security operations center workflow to NASA FIRMS VIIRS NOAA-21 thermal detections. Google Cloud BigQuery and SQL support low-confidence filtering, alert identifiers and severity classification. An interactive dashboard combines a hotspot map, daily alert counts, mean fire radiative power (FRP) and a filterable event log for November 8-14, 2026.

The supplied snapshot contains 500 triaged events: 334 High and 166 Medium/Low. Peak FRP is 639.46 MW and mean brightness temperature is 343.6 K. Using a reported FRP baseline mean of 78.48 MW and standard deviation of 52.30 MW, the prototype flags 20 readings at Z >= 2. The peak event has Z approximately +10.73.

The project supports Earth System Trend Detective by showing where thermal detections occur, how daily observations vary, and which readings warrant investigation. Z-scores provide exploratory outlier screening, rather than validated p-values or evidence of a significant time trend. Next steps include longer baselines, formal trend testing, scheduled ingestion and webhook alerts.
details:
What It Does & How It Works Instead of plotting thousands of raw satellite dots equally on a map, EarthSOC Sentinel treats thermal detections like security alerts that need to be filtered, ranked, and verified before an analyst investigates them.

  • Cloud Data & SQL Triage: We loaded NASA FIRMS VIIRS NOAA-21 thermal detections into Google Cloud BigQuery (earthsoc-sentinel.nasa_telemetry.raw_firms_detections) and wrote a SQL triage query (soc_triage_engine.sql) that removes low-confidence sensor noise (confidence != 'l'), assigns unique UUID alert IDs, formats coordinates and UTC orbital pass times, and ranks events into CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, and LOWtiers for Tier-2 review or active monitoring.
  • Daily Patterns & Z-Score Outlier Screening: Across our 500-event snapshot from November 8–14, 2026 (334High and 166 Medium/Low alerts), we calculated the baseline Fire Radiative Power mean (μ=78.48 MWμ=78.48 MW) and standard deviation (σ=52.30 MWσ=52.30 MW), then computed an individual Z-score (Z=(FRP−78.48)/52.30 for every reading. As an exploratory outlier screen, readings at Z≥+2.0σZ≥+2.0σ flag 20 unusually intense thermal surges peaking at 639.46 MW639.46 MW (Z≈+10.73Z≈+10.73).
  • Interactive Web Console: We built the front-end dashboard (dashboard.html) with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet.js, and Chart.js and hosted it on GitHub Pages. Analysts can inspect hotspot locations on a dark-mode map, track daily alert volume alongside mean FRP over time, and filter the 500-event log by severity level.

Tools, Languages & AI Assistance

  • Tech Stack: Google Cloud BigQuery, SQL, Zsh/AWK, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet.js, Chart.js, and GitHub Pages.
  • AI Tool Disclosure: We used Google Gemini as a coding assistant to help structure our BigQuery SQL query, build script, and HTML/JavaScript dashboard layout, and OpenAI ChatGPT to assist with drafting and formatting our presentation slides. Our team handled the NASA FIRMS data ingestion, BigQuery execution, statistical checks, and GitHub Pages deployment.

Who It Helps & Next Steps This prototype gives emergency-response analysts, agencies, and environmental researchers a transparent review queue for spotting unusual thermal activity. Future steps include longer multi-week baselines, formal statistical trend tests, scheduled BigQuery ingestion, and automated webhook alerts.
